divisions.name: Practice Management
divisions.description: Assesses objectives related to the management of architectural practice, including professional ethics, fiduciary responsibilities, business structure, financial health, risk mitigation, and practice-wide delivery of services.

objectives.text: Assess resources within the practice (staffing, hardware, software, training)
Apply regulations and requirements governing the work environment (OSHA, ADA, FMLA, labor laws, insurance)
Apply ethical standards to comply with accepted principles (NCARB Model Rules of Conduct & AIA Code of Ethics)
Apply appropriate Standard of Care

sections.title: Section 2: Finances, Risk, & Development of Practice

objectives.text: Evaluate the financial well-being of the practice (Net Multiplier, Overhead Rate, Utilization, Profit/Loss, Balance Sheets)
Identify practice policies and methodologies to reduce risk and liabilities
Select and apply legal and business structures for the practice (Sole Proprietorship, LLP, LLC, S-Corp, C-Corp, Joint Venture)
Determine optimal delivery methods and contract types for client proposals (DBB, DB, CMAR, IPD)
Analyze client requests (RFP/RFQ) and establish service scope and fee proposals
Manage third-party consultant relationships at a practice level
Evaluate research, evidence-based design, and post-occupancy data to inform practice
Establish BIM, CAD, QA/QC, and office-wide documentation standards

divisions.name: Project Management
divisions.description: Assesses objectives related to the management of architectural projects, including organizing principles, contract administration (AIA B101, A201, C401), work planning, Critical Path scheduling, budget compliance, and quality control.

objectives.text: Determine criteria required to assemble project team
Allocate and manage project resources and staff hours across phases
Develop and maintain project work plan (Gantt charts, task dependencies)
Determine criteria required to develop and maintain project schedule (Critical Path Method, float)
Determine appropriate communication to project team (owner, contractor, consultants, internal staff)
Evaluate and verify adherence to owner/architect agreement (AIA B101-2017)
Interpret key elements of architect/consultant agreement (AIA C401-2017)
Interpret key elements of owner/contractor agreement (AIA A101 & A201-2017)
Integrate owner's specialty consultants into project work
Evaluate compliance with construction budget (AIA B101 Article 6 cost of the work)
Evaluate and address changes in scope of work and scope creep
Evaluate project documentation to support specified delivery method
Identify and conform with AHJ requirements to obtain approvals
Apply procedures required for adherence to laws and regulations
Identify steps in maintaining project QA/QC and reducing risk/liabilities
Perform quality control reviews and interdisciplinary coordination (MEP/Structural clashes)
Evaluate management of the design process to maintain design integrity

divisions.name: Programming & Analysis
divisions.description: Assesses objectives related to the evaluation of project requirements, constraints, and opportunities, including site analysis, soil/topography, climate passive design, zoning ordinances (FAR, setbacks), IBC occupancy/allowable area, and spatial programming.

objectives.text: Analyze site-specific environmental conditions (climate, solar path, wind rose, acoustics, floodplains)
Evaluate neighborhood context, historic preservation standards, and urban fabric
Identify environmental remediation requirements (brownfields, asbestos, radon, lead, wetlands)
Identify and apply zoning and land-use requirements (FAR, setbacks, lot coverage, parking, variances)
Identify and apply building codes and accessibility standards at programming phase (IBC Ch. 3, 5, 6, 10 & ADA)
Evaluate geotechnical, soil bearing, grading contours, storm drainage, and utilities
Synthesize site circulation, access, views, and topography into programmatic site diagrams
Establish space requirements, net-to-gross efficiency ratios, and adjacency matrices
Evaluate existing buildings for adaptive reuse and historic preservation treatments
Develop preliminary project budgets and life-cycle cost feasibility analyses

divisions.name: Project Planning & Design
divisions.description: The most integrative ARE 5.0 division. Focuses on schematic design synthesis, selecting and coordinating structural, mechanical (HVAC), electrical, plumbing, acoustics, and building envelope systems with IBC fire/life safety codes and project cost constraints.

objectives.text: Determine building orientation, solar shading, passive heating/cooling, and daylighting strategies
Integrate sustainable site design, stormwater management, and microclimate controls
Apply IBC means of egress (common path, travel distance, dead-end corridors, exit width, stair enclosures)
Apply occupancy classifications, fire-resistance ratings, mixed-use separations, and IECC energy codes
Select and size HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lighting, and fire suppression systems
Select structural gravity and lateral force-resisting systems (shear walls, braced frames, moment frames, foundations)
Evaluate building envelope assemblies, glazing, roofing, and acoustical assemblies (STC/NRC/IIC)

sections.title: Section 4: Project Integration of Program & Systems

objectives.text: Synthesize structural grid, mechanical distribution trees, cores, and spatial program into schematic design
Evaluate design alternatives for life safety, accessibility, structural efficiency, and sustainability
Evaluate schematic cost estimates, location/inflation adjustments, and value engineering trade-offs

divisions.name: Project Development & Documentation
divisions.description: Focuses on moving from schematic design into Design Development and Construction Documents: detailing wall assemblies, vapor/air/water barriers, flashing, structural connections, MEP coordination, CSI MasterFormat 3-Part Specifications, and detailed cost estimates.

sections.title: Section 1: Integration of Building Materials & Systems

objectives.text: Resolve wall, roof, foundation, and curtain wall assembly details (flashing, weep holes, thermal bridges, vapor retarders)
Select material finishes, galvanic corrosion protection, expansion/control joints, and firestopping details
Coordinate structural connections, slab penetrations, and MEP equipment clearances
Produce and coordinate architectural floor plans, reflected ceiling plans, building sections, and schedules
Verify interdisciplinary coordination across structural, mechanical, electrical, and plumbing drawings
Organize Project Manual using CSI MasterFormat (50 Divisions) and CSI 3-Part SectionFormat (General, Products, Execution)
Verify detailed code compliance (ADA mounting heights, stair handrails/guards, UL fire-rated assemblies, IECC U-factors)
Perform detailed quantity takeoffs and unit-cost construction estimates at CD phase

divisions.name: Construction & Evaluation
divisions.description: Assesses objectives related to bidding and negotiation, construction contract administration (AIA A201, G701, G702/G703, G704), site observation, shop drawing/submittal review, RFIs, payment applications, non-conforming work, project closeout, and post-occupancy evaluation.

objectives.text: Interpret the architect's roles and responsibilities during bidding/preconstruction by delivery method (Addenda, AIA A701)
Analyze criteria for selecting contractors, bid bonds, performance/payment bonds, and alternates
Analyze aspects of the contract or design to adjust project costs when bids exceed budget
Evaluate the architect's role during site visits (design intent vs. contractor's means and methods)
Evaluate construction conformance with contract documents, codes, and testing standards (slump/cylinder tests, soils)
Determine construction progress against CPM schedule and Schedule of Values
Determine appropriate supplemental documentation (ASI G710, Change Order G701, CCD G714, Proposal Request G709)
Evaluate submittals including shop drawings, samples, mock-ups, product data, and independent test results
Evaluate contractor's Application and Certificate for Payment (AIA G702/G703, retainage, stored materials)
Evaluate responses to non-conformance with contract documents (rejecting work, uncovering work, claims)
Apply procedural concepts to complete closeout (Punch list, Substantial Completion G704, Final Completion, Release of Liens G706)
Evaluate building design and performance (Commissioning, Post-Occupancy Evaluation, IAQ / Sick Building Syndrome)

resources.title: AIA B101-2017 Owner-Architect Agreement Excerpts
resources.content:
AIA DOCUMENT B101-2017 EXCERPTS:
• Article 3.1: Basic Services include Structural, Mechanical, and Electrical engineering services (normally retained by the Architect via AIA C401-2017). Geotechnical engineering and Land Surveying are provided by the Owner under Article 5.
• Article 4.1 (Supplemental Services): Programming, LEED Certification, Measured Drawings, Acoustic Design, and Post-Occupancy Evaluation are Supplemental Services only provided if designated in Section 4.1.1.
• Article 6 (Cost of the Work):
  - Cost of the Work includes contractor's general conditions, overhead, and profit at current market rates, plus a reasonable allowance for contingencies.
  - Cost of the Work DOES NOT include the compensation of the Architect, cost of the land, rights-of-way, or financing costs (Sec. 6.1).
  - Sec. 6.7: If the lowest bona fide bid exceeds the Owner's budget for the Cost of the Work, the Owner may: (1) increase the budget; (2) authorize rebidding within a reasonable time; (3) terminate the contract; or (4) cooperate with the Architect in revising the project scope/quality. If option (4) is selected, the Architect shall modify the Construction Documents WITHOUT additional compensation as their sole responsibility.

ZONING ORDINANCE EXCERPT (DISTRICT C-3):
• Site Dimensions: 150 ft (East-West frontage) × 200 ft (North-South depth) = 30,000 SF Total Lot Area
• Maximum Floor Area Ratio (FAR): 3.0

resources.title: IBC Chapter 3 & Chapter 5 Occupancy & Incidental Use
resources.content:
INTERNATIONAL BUILDING CODE (IBC) EXCERPTS:
• Section 303.1.2 (Small Assembly Spaces): A room or space used for assembly purposes that is less than 750 square feet in area and accessory to another occupancy shall be classified as a Group B occupancy or as part of that occupancy.
• Section 508.2 (Accessory Occupancies): Aggregate accessory occupancies shall not occupy more than 10% of the building area of the story in which they are located.
• Section 509 (Incidental Uses): Spaces listed in Table 509 (e.g., furnace rooms > 400,000 Btu/hr, laboratories, laundry rooms > 100 SF) shall not occupy more than 10% of the building area of the story in which they are located and require either a fire barrier separation or automatic sprinkler system.
• Typical Building Net-to-Gross Efficiency Ratios:
  - Commercial Office: 75% – 80%
  - Healthcare / Hospital / Laboratory: 55% – 65%
  - Restaurant / Culinary: 65% – 70%

caseStudies.title: Case Study: Great Lakes Performing Arts & Academic Center — Systems Integration
caseStudies.scenario: An architect is developing the schematic design for a 3-story, 90,000 GSF Performing Arts and Academic Center in Milwaukee, WI (ASHRAE Climate Zone 6A — Cold). The building includes a 600-seat recital hall (clear span 80 ft), acoustic rehearsal studios, and multi-story classroom wings.

resources.title: Mechanical, Structural & Acoustical Design Criteria
resources.content:
ENGINEERING SYSTEMS MATRIX:
1. HVAC Selection Criteria:
   • Recital Hall (High Occupancy, Strict Acoustic Criteria NC-15 to NC-20): Requires single-zone Constant Air Volume (CAV) or low-velocity displacement ventilation with remote air-handling unit, lined ductwork, vibration isolators, and sound attenuators.
   • Classroom & Office Wing (Variable Occupancy & Diverse Solar Orientations): Variable Air Volume (VAV) with reheat or Dedicated Outdoor Air System (DOAS) + chilled beams/hydronic radiant panels.
   • Hydronic Piping: Two-pipe reverse-return system provides equal total pipe length (supply + return) to every terminal unit, balancing flow and head loss naturally.
2. Structural Span & Lateral Criteria:
   • 80-ft Clear Span Recital Hall Roof: Long-span steel trusses (depth ~ L/10 to L/12 = 6.5 to 8 ft) or deep plate girders.
   • Lateral Force-Resisting System: Eccentrically Braced Frames (EBF) or Special Reinforced Concrete Shear Walls around the stage tower and egress cores.
3. Acoustical Reverberation Time (Sabine Formula):
   • RT60 = 0.049 × V / A  (where V = room volume in cu. ft., A = total absorption in Sabins = Σ(S × α)).
   • Target RT60: Speech/Drama = 0.8–1.1 sec; Chamber Music/Recital = 1.4–1.8 sec; Symphony/Organ = 1.8–2.2 sec.

resources.title: IBC Chapter 10 Means of Egress & Fire Protection
resources.content:
IBC CHAPTER 10 EGRESS REQUIREMENTS (FULLY SPRINKLERED - NFPA 13):
• Occupant Load Factors (Table 1004.5):
  - Assembly fixed seats: Number of fixed seats
  - Assembly unconcentrated (tables & chairs): 15 net SF/occupant
  - Assembly standing space: 5 net SF/occupant
  - Educational classrooms: 20 net SF/occupant
  - Business areas: 150 gross SF/occupant
• Number of Exits (Table 1006.3.2):
  - 1 to 500 occupants: Minimum 2 exits
  - 501 to 1,000 occupants: Minimum 3 exits
  - > 1,000 occupants: Minimum 4 exits
• Exit Separation (Remoteness - Sec. 1007.1.1):
  - Non-sprinklered: >= 1/2 diagonal dimension of area served
  - Fully Sprinklered (NFPA 13): >= 1/3 diagonal dimension of area served
• Egress Width Factors (Sec. 1005.3 - Sprinklered without voice alarm vs. with voice alarm):
  - Stairways: 0.3 inches per occupant (standard) / 0.2 in (sprinklered + emergency voice/alarm)
  - Other egress components (doors/corridors/ramps): 0.2 inches per occupant (standard) / 0.15 in (sprinklered + voice/alarm)

resources.title: AIA A201-2017 General Conditions of the Contract for Construction

AIA DOCUMENT A201-2017 KEY ADMINISTRATION CLAUSES:
• Sec. 3.7.4 (Concealed or Unknown Conditions): If the Contractor encounters subsurface or otherwise concealed physical conditions that differ materially from the Contract Documents, the Contractor shall promptly notify the Owner and Architect BEFORE conditions are disturbed and within 14 days after first observance. The Architect will promptly investigate and recommend an equitable adjustment by Change Order if warranted.

questions.section: Section 2: Finances, Risk, & Development of Practice
questions.source: Hyperfine PcM/PjM Assignment 1 & Case Study CS-PCM-1
questions.stem: Refer to the Studio Vesper LLP Q3 Financial Statement in the Case Study resources. Based on Net Operating Revenue (NOR) of $3,400,000 and Direct Salary Expense (DSE) of $1,000,000, what is the firm's Net Multiplier? (Round to two decimal places, e.g., 2.85)
questions.explanation: Net Multiplier = Net Operating Revenue (NOR) / Direct Salary Expense (DSE). From the financial statement, NOR = Gross Revenue ($4,250,000) - Consultant Pass-Throughs ($850,000) = $3,400,000. Dividing $3,400,000 by Direct Salary Expense ($1,000,000) yields a Net Multiplier of 3.40. Because the firm's Break-Even Rate is 1 + (Overhead $1,800,000 / Direct Labor $1,000,000) = 2.80, a Net Multiplier of 3.40 exceeds Break-Even (2.80) and indicates a profitable practice (AHPP Section 7.2 & Hyperfine Assignment 1).

questions.stem: Using the Studio Vesper LLP Q3 Financial Statement, what is the firm's Overhead Rate (expressed as a ratio of Total Overhead to Direct Salary Expense) and resulting Break-Even Rate?

options.text: Overhead Rate = 1.55; Break-Even Rate = 2.55
Overhead Rate = 1.80; Break-Even Rate = 2.80
Overhead Rate = 2.40; Break-Even Rate = 3.40
Overhead Rate = 0.75; Break-Even Rate = 1.75

questions.explanation: Overhead Rate = Total Indirect/General Overhead Expenses ($1,800,000) / Total Direct Labor ($1,000,000) = 1.80 (or 180%). Break-Even Rate = 1.00 (for direct labor dollar) + Overhead Rate (1.80) = 2.80. Every $1.00 spent on direct billable labor requires $2.80 in Net Operating Revenue just to break even.

questions.source: Hyperfine PcM/PjM Assignment 2 (Insurance)
questions.stem: Studio Vesper carried a $2,000,000 Professional Liability (claims-made) policy with a $100,000 deductible when it designed a library in 2023. After construction completed, the firm reduced its claims-made policy to $1,000,000 coverage with a $50,000 deductible while maintaining continuous coverage. Today, a negligence claim is settled against the firm for $1,750,000. How much is Studio Vesper responsible for paying out of pocket?
questions.explanation: Professional Liability (Errors & Omissions) policies are written on a 'claims-made' basis, meaning the policy limits in effect AT THE TIME THE CLAIM IS FILED govern, not the policy in effect when the design took place. Under the current $1,000,000 / $50,000 policy: first, the architect pays the $50,000 deductible; second, the insurer pays up to the $1,000,000 policy limit; and the architect must pay the remaining $750,000 uninsured excess ($1,750,000 - $1,000,000 = $750,000) plus the $50,000 deductible = $800,000 total out of pocket (Hyperfine Assignment 2).

General Partnership
Unincorporated Joint Venture

questions.explanation: Both a Limited Liability Company (LLC) and a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) provide pass-through taxation (avoiding C-Corp double taxation) and shield owners' personal assets from general business debts and the malpractice of other partners (note: in all entities, an architect always remains personally liable for their own professional negligence/torts). Sole proprietorships and General Partnerships have unlimited personal liability.
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (Business Organization)

questions.source: NCARB Model Rules of Conduct & PCM Study Guide RMS
questions.stem: During a municipal zoning board hearing for a controversial commercial development, an architect who serves on a local civic preservation committee speaks publicly against the project. The architect was recently hired by an adjacent property owner to evaluate how the development will impact neighborhood shadows. Under the NCARB Model Rules of Conduct, what is the architect's ethical obligation?

options.text: The architect must recuse themselves from speaking because architects may not criticize another architect's work publicly.
The architect may make public statements on architectural issues, provided they disclose on whose behalf they are speaking and any financial compensation/interest.
The architect must obtain written consent from the project's architect of record before addressing the zoning board.
No disclosure is required because civic committee testimony is protected under First Amendment public comment.

questions.explanation: Under NCARB Model Rules of Conduct (Rule 2.3) and AIA Code of Ethics Rule 2.103, an architect making a public statement on an architectural issue must disclose when they are being compensated for making the statement or when they have an economic interest in the issue.
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (3 Tiers of AIA Code of Ethics & 5 Model Rules of Conduct)

questions.source: PCM Study Guide RMS & PPI2Pass PcM
questions.stem: Match each federal employment regulation or insurance policy to the minimum firm size threshold or claim scenario it governs.

targets.label: Requires reasonable accommodations for qualified employees with disabilities
Mandates up to 12 weeks of job-protected unpaid medical/family leave
Requires group health plan continuation coverage after employee termination
Covers a client who slips and falls on the stairs inside the architect's office

questions.explanation: Federal employment law thresholds tested on PcM: OSHA (1+ employees, recordkeeping at 10+), FLSA (all employers), Title VII Civil Rights & ADA (15+ employees), ADEA Age Discrimination & COBRA (20+ employees), FMLA Family and Medical Leave Act (50+ employees). A client injured slipping in the architect's office is a non-professional premises injury covered by Commercial General Liability (CGL).
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (Human Resources & Legal Requirements) & Hyperfine Assignment 2

questions.source: Hyperfine PcM/PjM & Schiff Hardin Lectures
questions.stem: To prevail in a professional negligence (tort) claim against an architect, the plaintiff must prove which FOUR legal elements?

options.text: Duty: The architect owed a legal duty to conform to the professional Standard of Care
Breach: The architect failed to meet that Standard of Care
Intent: The architect willfully intended to cause financial harm to the owner
Cause (Proximate Cause): The breach directly caused the resulting defect or injury
Damages: Actual quantifiable harm or loss occurred as a result
Privity of Contract: A direct signed contract existed between the plaintiff and architect

questions.explanation: The 4 required elements of a negligence claim in tort law are: (1) Duty, (2) Breach of the Standard of Care, (3) Proximate Cause, and (4) Actual Damages. Intent is not required for negligence, and tort claims often arise from third parties without privity of contract.
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (Elements of Claim/Negligence) & Schiff Hardin Lectures

questions.source: AIA B101 / B195 & Black Spectacles PcM
questions.stem: A hospital system wants to build a complex proton-therapy facility with aggressive schedule targets, early trade contractor input during conceptual design, shared financial risk/reward pools, and a multi-party agreement signed jointly by the Owner, Architect, and Constructor. Which project delivery method and AIA contract family are most appropriate?

options.text: Design-Bid-Build using AIA A101 and B101
Construction Manager as Adviser (CMa) using AIA C132 and B132
Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) using the AIA C191 Multi-Party Agreement or A195/B195 family
Bridging Design-Build using AIA A141

questions.explanation: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD) unites the Owner, Architect, and Constructor under a single multi-party agreement (AIA C191) or transitional IPD agreements (A195/B195/A295) featuring shared risk and reward, early contractor involvement from conceptualization, and collaborative BIM workflows.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 2.pdf & NCARB Handbook p. 122

questions.source: PPI Review Manual Div 2 & Case Study CS-PJM-1
questions.stem: Refer to the Riverwalk Innovation Hub Case Study (CS-PJM-1). When the Construction Documents are put out to bid, the lowest bona fide bid comes in 18% above the Owner's budget for the Cost of the Work. The Owner directs the Architect to revise the Construction Documents to reduce the project scope and bring the project within budget. Under AIA Document B101-2017 Section 6.7, how is the Architect compensated for modifying the Construction Documents?

options.text: The Architect bills the Owner hourly as an Additional Service under Article 4.2.
The Architect must modify the Construction Documents without additional compensation as the Architect's sole responsibility.
The Architect and Owner split the redesign fee 50/50 unless market escalation exceeded 10%.
The Architect is only required to modify the documents without compensation if a Construction Manager was hired.

questions.explanation: Under AIA B101-2017 Section 6.7, if the Owner's budget for the Cost of the Work is exceeded by the lowest bona fide bid or negotiated proposal, and the Owner chooses option 6.6.4 (cooperate in revising the Project scope and quality as required to reduce the Cost of the Work), the Architect shall modify the Architectural Construction Documents as necessary to comply with the Owner's budget WITHOUT additional compensation, and such modification is the limit of the Architect's responsibility.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 2.pdf (Contracts) & AIA B101-2017 Art. 6

questions.source: Hyperfine Assignment 21 & Case Study CS-PJM-1
questions.stem: Refer to the Critical Path Method (CPM) Network Data in Case Study CS-PJM-1. Path A (Envelope & Structure) takes 30 weeks, Path B (MEP Rough-In) takes 27 weeks, and Path C (Elevator Procurement) takes 22 weeks. How many weeks of Total Float does Path B (MEP Rough-In) have before it delays the overall project completion date?
questions.explanation: The Critical Path is the longest sequence of dependent activities through the network, which determines the shortest possible project duration: Path A = 30 weeks. Total Float for Path B = Critical Path Duration (30 weeks) - Path B Duration (27 weeks) = 3 weeks of float.
questions.reference: hyperfine_pcm-pjm-sample-assignments.pdf (Assignment 21: Schedules & CPM)

questions.source: PPI Review Manual Div 2 & AIA B101-2017
questions.stem: Under a standard AIA Document B101-2017 agreement, which THREE of the following services or consultants are provided by the Owner (Article 5) or designated as Supplemental Services (Article 4.1), rather than included in the Architect's Basic Services (Article 3)?

options.text: Geotechnical engineering and soil borings
Normal structural, mechanical, and electrical engineering design
LEED / sustainable design certification documentation
Boundary, topographic, and utility land survey
Reviewing Contractor's Applications for Payment (AIA G702)
Preparing Design Development outline specifications

questions.explanation: Under AIA B101-2017: Geotechnical engineering (Sec. 5.4) and Land Surveys (Sec. 5.3) are furnished by the Owner; Sustainable Project Services / LEED Certification (Sec. 4.1.1.22 / E204) is a Supplemental Service. Normal structural, mechanical, and electrical engineering, DD outline specs, and reviewing G702 payment applications are part of the Architect's Basic Services under Article 3.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 2.pdf & NCARB Handbook p. 84

questions.source: AIA C401-2017 & PPI Review Manual Div 2
questions.stem: An architect hires a structural engineer using AIA Document C401-2017 (Standard Form of Agreement Between Architect and Consultant). The Owner has withheld payment from the Architect for the Design Development phase due to a dispute strictly concerning the Architect's interior atrium layout (unrelated to the structural engineer's work). Under AIA C401-2017, what is the Architect's obligation regarding payment to the structural engineer?

options.text: The Architect must pay the Consultant within 7 days after receiving the Consultant's invoice, regardless of whether the Owner has paid the Architect.
AIA C401 contains a 'pay-when-paid' provision where the Architect pays the Consultant promptly after receiving payment from the Owner, unless nonpayment is the fault of the Architect.
The Consultant must file a mechanic's lien directly against the Architect's firm bank account.
The Owner is contractually required to pay the structural engineer directly under AIA A201.

questions.explanation: Under AIA C401-2017 Section 11.6, payments to the Consultant shall be made promptly after the Architect is paid by the Owner under the Prime Agreement. However, the Architect must exert reasonable and diligent efforts to collect payment from the Owner, and if the Owner withholds payment solely due to the Architect's fault (not the Consultant's), the Architect remains responsible to the Consultant.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 2.pdf (Architect/Consultant Agreement C401)

questions.source: AIA B101 Article 7 & Hyperfine PcM/PjM
questions.stem: Under AIA Document B101-2017 Article 7 (Copyrights and Licenses), who owns the Instruments of Service (drawings, specifications, and BIM models), and what happens if the Owner terminates the Architect for convenience and hires an unlicensed drafter to finish the project using the Architect's drawings?

options.text: The Owner owns the Instruments of Service upon paying the Schematic Design invoice.

The Architect and the Architect's consultants retain ownership and copyright of their Instruments of Service; the Owner's nonexclusive license is contingent on full payment and executing a termination licensing fee/indemnification.
Copyright automatically transfers to the General Contractor once a building permit is issued.
Instruments of Service enter the public domain once filed with the municipal building department.

questions.explanation: Under AIA B101-2017 Section 7.2 and 7.3, the Architect and the Architect's consultants are deemed the authors and owners of their respective Instruments of Service and retain all common law, statutory, and other reserved rights, including copyrights. The Architect grants the Owner a nonexclusive license solely for constructing, using, and maintaining the Project, conditioned upon the Owner timely paying all sums due.
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (Instruments of Service) & AIA B101 Art. 7

questions.source: PPI Review Manual Div 2 (p. 6-15 Wood Veneer & Specs)
questions.stem: During a Design Development quality control review for an executive boardroom, the project manager checks the architectural woodwork drawings to ensure the wood veneer grain pattern will appear as a continuous, symmetrical mirror-image pattern across adjacent panels (like opening the pages of a book), and that veneers come from a single log (flitch). Which veneer matching method should be specified?

options.text: Slip match with rotary-cut veneer
Book match from a single sequence-numbered flitch
Random match with plain-sliced veneer
Running match from multiple logs

questions.explanation: Book matching turns every alternate sheet of veneer from a flitch over (like pages of a book), producing a symmetrical mirror-image grain joint at every seam. Specifying architectural-grade sequence-matched panels from a single flitch ensures consistent color and grain across the boardroom.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 2.pdf (Project Execution & Quality Control)

questions.source: NCARB Handbook Sample Item & PjM Case Study
questions.stem: Refer to the Fee Breakdown in Case Study CS-PJM-1. The total Basic Services fee is $1,200,000. The firm has completed 100% of Schematic Design (15%), 100% of Design Development (20%), and 50% of Construction Documents (40% weight). If the firm has already billed and collected $420,000 for SD and DD, what dollar amount should be billed on the current invoice for the 50% completion of Construction Documents?
questions.explanation: Total CD Phase Fee = 40% of $1,200,000 = $480,000. At 50% completion of Construction Documents, the earned fee for the CD phase is 0.50 × $480,000 = $240,000. (Cumulative earned to date = $180k SD + $240k DD + $240k CD = $660,000; less $420,000 previously billed = $240,000 due).
questions.reference: NCARB Handbook-ARE-5-Guidelines-AUG 2024.pdf (PjM Objective 3.1)

questions.source: PCM Study Guide RMS & AIA B101 Art. 8
questions.stem: Under standard AIA Document B101-2017 and A201-2017 agreements, if a claim or dispute between the Owner and Architect cannot be resolved by direct negotiation, what is the mandatory condition precedent before initiating binding dispute resolution (arbitration or litigation)?

options.text: Filing a formal complaint with the state architectural licensing board
Mediation administered by the American Arbitration Association (AAA)
Mini-trial before a Dispute Review Board
Obtaining a Declaratory Judgment in federal court

questions.explanation: Under AIA B101-2017 Article 8 (Section 8.2) and AIA A201-2017 Article 15, any claim subject to, but not resolved by, mediation shall be subject to the method of binding dispute resolution selected in the agreement (Arbitration, Litigation, or Other). Mediation is a mandatory condition precedent to binding dispute resolution.
questions.reference: PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (Dispute Resolution Procedures)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 1)
questions.stem: An architect is designing a house for a client in a cold climate where the annual wind rose indicates the highest frequency of strong winter winds (over 20 mph) comes from the northwest and west, with prevailing warmer breezes from the south-southeast. Which THREE sides of the house should have minimal glazing and windbreaks to prevent cold winter air infiltration?

options.text: North
South
East
West
Southeast
Northwest

questions.explanation: In a cold climate, the majority of glazing should face south (optimally 5° to 25° east of south) to maximize passive solar heat gain. Based on northern hemisphere solar geometry and the wind rose showing strong winter winds from the northwest and west, windows should be minimized and windbreaks planted on the North (A), West (D), and Northwest (F) exposures (Brown & DeKay, Sun, Wind & Light, p. 13-14).
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 1, p. 33 & p. 66)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 2)
questions.stem: A topographic map of a building site has been lost, forcing the architect to calculate the vertical drop of a storm drain pipe running from a hilly rural site to the center of the street. The plumbing consultant has requested a 7.5% slope on the 315-foot-long pipe running 8'-0" below grade to ensure water in the line does not freeze. What is the total vertical drop (rise) of the pipe?
questions.explanation: Using the slope formula: Slope = Rise / Run. Note that the 8'-0" burial depth is a distractor that does not change the vertical drop over the 315 ft run. Convert 7.5% to a decimal (0.075) and multiply by the 315 ft run: Rise = 0.075 × 315 ft = 23.625 ft ≈ 23.63 ft (Russ, Site Planning and Design Handbook, p. 129-137).
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 2, p. 33 & p. 66)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 4)
questions.stem: A client has approached an architect to build a university-affiliated research laboratory building that includes two small, 700-square-foot lecture halls making up less than 10% of the total floor area of the story, used for college overflow seminars. According to the International Building Code (IBC Section 303.1.2 & Section 508/509), how should the building occupancy be classified?

options.text: Group A-3 (Assembly)
Mixed Occupancy: Group B (Business) & Group A-3 (Assembly)
Group B (Business)
Group E (Educational)

questions.explanation: Under IBC Chapter 3 (Section 303.1.2), a room or space used for assembly purposes that is less than 750 square feet in area and accessory to another occupancy shall be classified as a Group B occupancy or as part of that occupancy. Furthermore, university/college laboratories and classrooms above the 12th grade are classified as Group B (Business), not Group E (which applies through 12th grade). Therefore, the entire building is classified as Group B.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 4, p. 33 & p. 66)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 10)
questions.stem: A new retail center is planned on a 100 ft × 75 ft site with a 15-foot setback on each side. According to the local zoning code, the site has a maximum Floor Area Ratio (FAR) of 3.0. The owner requires an estimated building net-to-gross efficiency ratio of 75%. What is the largest Net Floor Area (in SF) that the developer could build on this site?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is always calculated using the TOTAL LOT AREA, not the setback buildable footprint (the 15-ft setback is a classic ARE distractor unless limiting height/stories!). Total Lot Area = 100 ft × 75 ft = 7,500 SF. Step 2: Maximum Gross Floor Area (GFA) = FAR 3.0 × 7,500 SF = 22,500 GSF. Step 3: Maximum Net Floor Area (NFA) at 75% efficiency = 22,500 GSF × 0.75 = 16,875 NSF (Buildable footprint is 70 ft × 45 ft = 3,150 SF, so 22,500 GSF would require 8 stories).
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 10, p. 34)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 13)
questions.stem: An architect is programming a new restaurant with a 5,550 SF kitchen, a 12,600 SF dining area, 4 water closets (2 male, 2 female at 50 SF each = 200 SF), a 1,500 SF waiting area, a basement mechanical room of 8,500 SF, and a rooftop mechanical penthouse for kitchen hoods of 1,275 SF. Assuming net programmable area includes the kitchen, dining, and waiting areas (19,650 SF) out of the total 29,625 GSF, what is the restaurant's building efficiency ratio?
questions.explanation: Net Programmable Area (Assigned Spaces) = 5,550 SF (kitchen) + 12,600 SF (dining) + 1,500 SF (waiting) = 19,650 NSF. Unassigned/Gross-only support spaces = 200 SF (restrooms) + 8,500 SF (basement mechanical) + 1,275 SF (rooftop mechanical penthouse) = 9,975 SF. Total Gross Area = 19,650 + 9,975 = 29,625 GSF. Building Efficiency Ratio = 19,650 NSF / 29,625 GSF = 66.33% ≈ 66.3%.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 13, p. 34)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 14)
questions.stem: An architect has four projects in the programming phase across different U.S. climate zones. Drag and place the optimal passive design strategy onto each geographical climate zone.
tokens: Narrow floor plan raised on piers with breezeway for cross-ventilation
High thermal mass walls with night-flush evaporative courtyard
Elongated East-West axis with deciduous southern shading & operable windows
Compact cube form minimizing surface area to volume ratio with triple glazing

targets.label: Hot-Humid (e.g., Miami, FL / New Orleans, LA)
targets.correctToken: Narrow floor plan raised on piers with breezeway for cross-ventilation

targets.label: Hot-Arid (e.g., Phoenix, AZ / Albuquerque, NM)
targets.correctToken: High thermal mass walls with night-flush evaporative courtyard

targets.label: Temperate (e.g., St. Louis, MO / Louisville, KY)
targets.correctToken: Elongated East-West axis with deciduous southern shading & operable windows

targets.label: Cold (e.g., Minneapolis, MN / Duluth, MN)
targets.correctToken: Compact cube form minimizing surface area to volume ratio with triple glazing

questions.explanation: Per Olgyay's Design with Climate and Sun, Wind & Light: Hot-Humid climates require continuous air movement and cross-ventilation via narrow floor plates; Hot-Arid climates have large diurnal temperature swings suited to high thermal mass and evaporative courtyards; Temperate climates balance solar gain and shading along an elongated E-W axis; Cold climates minimize conductive heat loss by minimizing surface-area-to-volume ratio.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 14, p. 4 & p. 34)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 8 — Hotspot)
questions.stem: An architect has contracted with a civil engineer for site grading on a hilly lot where a new House Addition (FFE 90'-0") is being built downhill from an Existing Garage (FFE 102'-6"). Click on the area of the topographic grading plan that indicates improper drainage pitching surface water directly against the new House Addition's north foundation wall.

targetZone.label: North Foundation Swale / Contour 95' Pitching Into Addition Wall

questions.explanation: Look at the 95' and 90' contour lines between the Existing Garage (FFE 102'-6") and the North wall of the House Addition (FFE 90'-0"). Because contour V-shapes pointing uphill indicate a valley/swale and V-shapes pointing downhill indicate a ridge, the contours between the garage and the north wall of the addition channel runoff directly against the house addition without a diversion swale pointing around the building.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 8 / Supplement #8, p. 3)

questions.source: Case Study CS-PA-1 (Mill District Mixed-Use)
questions.stem: Refer to the Mill District Mixed-Use Case Study (CS-PA-1) Zoning Ordinance and Geotechnical Report. Where should the architect locate the heaviest 5-story building mass on the site, and what is the maximum allowable ground-floor footprint (in SF) permitted on the 150 ft × 200 ft lot?

options.text: Northwest corner on spread footings; maximum footprint = 22,100 SF
Southeast quadrant on shallow spread footings (or deep piers to bedrock in NW); maximum footprint = 21,000 SF
Center of lot on a mat slab over peat; maximum footprint = 30,000 SF
Northwest corner on slab-on-grade; maximum footprint = 90,000 SF

questions.explanation: Step 1 (Soils): Boring B-1 (NW corner) has 22 ft of uncontrolled fill and soft organic peat (only 800 psf), requiring expensive deep foundations to bedrock, whereas Boring B-2 (SE quadrant) has medium-dense sand and gravel (3,500 psf) at 4 ft depth suitable for economical spread footings. Step 2 (Footprint): Total lot area = 150 × 200 = 30,000 SF. Setback envelope = (150 - 20) × (200 - 30) = 130 × 170 = 22,100 SF, BUT Maximum Lot Coverage is 70% of 30,000 SF = 21,000 SF. The stricter constraint (21,000 SF) governs!
questions.reference: Case Study CS-PA-1 & PA Walking the ARE 2.1

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 4 (Question 281)
questions.stem: An architect designed a bakery/coffee shop in Pittsburgh, PA, three years ago for an original construction cost of $300,000. The owner's sister wants to build an identical shop in Durham, NC, today. The location cost factor for Pittsburgh is 100, and the location factor for Durham is 75. Assuming a simple annual inflation rate of 2% per year over the 3 years (6% total inflation before compounding, or 6.12% compounded), what is the projected rough construction cost in Durham to the nearest thousand dollars? (Enter number, e.g., 238500 or 239000)
questions.explanation: Step 1: Adjust original cost for location index: $300,000 × (75 / 100) = $225,000. Step 2: Adjust for 3 years of inflation at 2%/yr: Using simple 6% escalation ($225,000 × 1.06) = $238,500 (or compounded $225,000 × (1.02)^3 = $238,772, which rounds to $239,000). Both $238,500 and $239,000 are accepted.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 4.pdf (Question 281, p. 4-3)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 4 (Question 283)
questions.stem: An architect is designing a 10-story building and is analyzing options for the cladding system. The building will utilize a prefabricated system with a variety of glass vision and spandrel panels. Although the structural grid of the building is very regular, to add visual interest to the facade, the panels will be a variety of custom sizes. Which cladding system is the most appropriate choice for this application?

options.text: Curtain wall stick system
Substrate-mounted composite metal and glass panels
Unitized curtain wall panel system
Metallic-finish EIFS system

questions.explanation: In a stick-built curtain wall system, mullions and rails are shipped loose and assembled piece-by-piece on site, making it much easier and more economical to accommodate varied panel sizes on a moderate 10-story building than a unitized panel system (which relies on high repetition of identical factory-assembled modules to justify tooling costs).
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 4.pdf (Question 283, p. 4-3)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 4 (Question 284)
questions.stem: What type of elevator system should be specified for high-speed vertical transportation in a 40-story high-rise office building?

options.text: Holeless hydraulic elevator
Gearless traction elevator
Geared traction elevator
Telescoping plunger hydraulic elevator

questions.explanation: Gearless traction elevators connect the drive sheave directly to a high-efficiency electric motor, achieving speeds of 500 to 2,000 feet per minute (fpm) and unlimited rise suitable for high-rise buildings (20+ stories). Hydraulic elevators are limited to ~5–6 stories (up to 60–70 ft) and 150–200 fpm; geared traction elevators serve mid-rise buildings up to ~15–20 stories (up to 500 fpm).
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 4.pdf (Question 284, p. 4-3)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 4 (Question 285)
questions.stem: An architect in Richmond, Virginia, has been asked to design a replacement roof for a hospital. The existing roof has a slope of approximately 1:12. The building supervisor requests a single-ply system that allows for additional rigid insulation to be installed below the membrane, resists hospital rooftop grease/exhaust chemicals, and accommodates paths of pavers for maintenance access to rooftop mechanical units. Which single-ply roofing system is most appropriate?

options.text: Ballasted loose-laid EPDM
Mechanically attached EPDM
Fully adhered Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) / TPO
Coal tar pitch built-up roof (BUR)

questions.explanation: A 1:12 slope is too steep for loose-laid ballasted roofing, and EPDM degrades when exposed to animal fats/grease from hospital kitchen exhausts. Fully adhered PVC (with heat-welded seams) handles a 1:12 slope, resists chemical/grease exhaust around mechanical units, allows additional insulation underneath, and supports walkway pads.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 4.pdf (Question 285, p. 4-4)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 4 (Question 288)
questions.stem: An architect is designing a high-end furniture and fine art gallery housed within a renovated historic bank building displaying $1,000,000+ of water-sensitive inventory. Which fire sprinkler system should be specified to prevent accidental water discharge from a damaged sprinkler head while still providing automatic fire suppression?

options.text: Wet-pipe sprinkler system
Deluge sprinkler system
Pre-action sprinkler system
Standpipe-only Class II hose cabinet system

questions.explanation: A Pre-action sprinkler system holds water back at an electrically operated pre-action valve and requires TWO independent events before water discharges: (1) activation of a supplemental smoke/heat detection system (which opens the valve and fills the pipes with water), AND (2) fusing of an individual sprinkler head over the fire. This prevents accidental water damage to fine art, archives, or server rooms if a pipe or sprinkler head is bumped.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 4.pdf (Question 288, p. 4-4)

questions.source: Case Study CS-PPD-1 (Great Lakes Performing Arts Center)
questions.stem: Refer to Case Study CS-PPD-1. The 600-seat recital hall is located on the second floor of the fully sprinklered (NFPA 13) building and also includes a 1,500 net SF lobby with unconcentrated tables and chairs. Using IBC Chapter 10 (without voice alarm reduction), what is the total occupant load of this level, the minimum number of required exits, and the minimum total stairway clear width?

options.text: 700 occupants; 2 exits required; 140 inches total stair width
700 occupants; 3 exits required; 210 inches total stair width
600 occupants; 3 exits required; 180 inches total stair width
750 occupants; 4 exits required; 225 inches total stair width

questions.explanation: Step 1 (Occupant Load): 600 fixed seats (600 occupants) + 1,500 NSF lobby / 15 NSF per occupant (100 occupants) = 700 total occupants. Step 2 (Number of Exits): Per IBC Table 1006.3.2, an occupant load of 501 to 1,000 requires a minimum of 3 exits. Step 3 (Stair Width): 700 occupants × 0.3 inches/occupant = 210 inches total stair width (or 70 inches per stair across 3 balanced stairs).
questions.reference: Case Study CS-PPD-1 & IBC Chapter 10

questions.source: Amber Book & School of PE Structural Systems
questions.stem: An architect is coordinating the lateral force-resisting system for a 6-story steel building in a high-seismic zone. Which THREE statements accurately describe the structural behavior of lateral systems and seismic configuration?

options.text: Eccentrically Braced Frames (EBF) combine the high elastic stiffness of braced frames with the ductile energy dissipation of moment frames via a shear link.
Locating the concrete shear wall core at one corner of an L-shaped floor plate eliminates torsional eccentricity.
A 'soft story' irregularity occurs when the lateral stiffness of a ground-floor retail lobby is less than 70% of the story above.
Rigid steel Moment Resisting Frames provide maximum architectural openness for windows and doors but experience greater lateral drift than Concentrically Braced Frames.
Seismic base shear is inversely proportional to the total dead weight (mass) of the building.
Seismic isolation bearings shorten the fundamental period of a rigid building so it resonates with high-frequency ground shaking.

questions.explanation: A, C, and D are correct: EBFs use a ductile 'fuse' link; a soft story has <70% of the stiffness of the story above; and Moment Frames allow open bays without diagonal braces at the cost of higher drift. B is false (a corner core creates severe torsion because the Center of Rigidity is far from the Center of Mass); E is false (Seismic force F = Mass × Acceleration, directly proportional to building weight); F is false (base isolators LENGTHEN the building's period to decouple it from ground motion).
questions.reference: FEMA 454 Designing for Earthquakes (ARE Resource Matrix 2.5)

questions.section: Section 1: Integration of Building Materials & Systems
questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 5 (Question 1, p. 3-1)
questions.stem: A designer is planning on using a hydronic distribution system to heat a building and needs to decide which piping configuration will be best for efficiency and balanced comfort control. To this end, the designer plans on supplying equal flow and fluid temperature to each radiator with equal total pipe run length to yield a naturally balanced return. Which piping system achieves this result?

options.text: One-pipe system
Two-pipe direct-return system
Two-pipe reverse-return system
Series perimeter loop system

questions.explanation: In a Two-pipe reverse-return hydronic system, the first terminal unit supplied is the last unit connected to the return main, so the combined length of supply + return piping (and friction head loss) is equal for every terminal unit in the loop, providing balanced flow and uniform supply water temperature.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf (Problem 1, p. 3-1 & Solution p. 3-6)

questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 5 (Question 2, p. 3-1)
questions.stem: Consider the location for a central mechanical air-handling system and its vertical distribution tree in a 10-story office building. Which of the following shaft/core locations should generally be AVOIDED because it creates the longest, most unequal horizontal duct runs?

options.text: Within internal circulation cores near the center of the floor plate
Split symmetrically into two service cores serving east and west zones
At one extreme narrow edge/corner of an elongated building floor plate
Between the internal core and the perimeter zone

questions.explanation: Locating a single vertical mechanical shaft at one extreme edge of an elongated floor plate forces horizontal supply and return ducts to span the entire length of the building, increasing static pressure loss, fan horsepower, and required ceiling plenum depth.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf (Problem 2, p. 3-1)

questions.source: Case Study CS-PDD-1 & Amber Book Envelope Detailing
questions.stem: Refer to the Prairie Health Pavilion Case Study (CS-PDD-1) for Cold Climate Zone 5A (Des Moines, IA). On the exterior brick veneer cavity wall section below, click on the layer where a Class I or II Vapor Retarder must be installed if interior cavity insulation is also present, to prevent warm humid indoor air from condensing inside the cold stud cavity during winter.

targetZone.label: Warm-in-Winter Side (Interior Face of Metal Studs Behind Interior Gypsum Board)

questions.explanation: Golden Rule of Vapor Retarders: Always place the low-perm vapor retarder on the WARM-IN-WINTER side of the dew point / insulation layer! In ASHRAE Climate Zone 5A (Des Moines, IA — Cold), the interior of the building is warm and humid in winter, so the vapor retarder belongs on the interior face of the studs just behind the interior gypsum board, while the exterior sheathing/WRB and exterior mineral wool remain vapor-permeable so the wall can dry outward.
questions.reference: Case Study CS-PDD-1 & PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf

questions.source: Case Study CS-PDD-1 (Galvanic Corrosion)
questions.stem: Refer to the Galvanic Series Guide in Case Study CS-PDD-1. An architect details copper through-wall flashing at a brick shelf angle. Which fastener material is compatible with copper flashing in the presence of moisture without experiencing rapid galvanic corrosion?

options.text: Hot-dip galvanized steel fasteners
Aluminum pop rivets
Copper, bronze, or Type 304/316 stainless steel fasteners
Uncoated carbon steel screws

questions.explanation: In the galvanic series, zinc (galvanized steel), aluminum, and carbon steel are strongly anodic relative to copper. Because fasteners have a very small surface area compared to the large cathodic copper flashing sheet, using galvanized or aluminum fasteners in copper causes rapid sacrificial corrosion of the fasteners. Only copper, brass/bronze, or passivated stainless steel fasteners should be used with copper flashing.
questions.reference: Case Study CS-PDD-1 & Architectural Graphic Standards

questions.source: Case Study CS-PDD-1 & CSI MasterFormat
questions.stem: Organize the following Project Manual items into their correct CSI MasterFormat Division or CSI 3-Part SectionFormat location.

targets.label: Instructions to Bidders (AIA A701) & Bid Bond Requirements
Administrative Submittal Procedures, Allowances, & Alternates Schedule
Fluid-Applied Air Barriers, Sheet Metal Flashing, & Joint Sealants
Field Quality Control Testing, Substrate Preparation, & Installation Tolerances

questions.explanation: Bidding documents and contract forms belong in Division 00; administrative procedures governing the work (submittals, allowances, alternates, closeout) belong in Division 01; air barriers, insulation, roofing, and flashing belong in Division 07; and field installation/testing requirements within any technical section belong in Part 3 — Execution.

questions.source: ADA Standards for Accessible Design & IBC Chapter 10
questions.stem: During a Construction Document QA/QC review of an exit stair and accessible restroom core, which THREE dimensions comply with the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design and the International Building Code (IBC)?

options.text: Stairway handrail top gripping surface mounted consistently between 34 inches and 38 inches above stair nosings
Accessible water closet centerline located 16 inches to 18 inches from the side wall (17 to 19 inches height AFF to top of seat)
Accessible ramp running slope of 1:8 (12.5%) for a 30-inch vertical rise
Minimum 60-inch diameter wheelchair turning space (or T-shaped turning space) inside accessible toilet rooms
Stair handrail extensions at the bottom of a stair flight extending 24 inches horizontally beyond the last riser
Guardrail height of 32 inches along an open atrium balcony in a commercial office building

questions.explanation: A, B, and D are code-compliant: handrails must be 34"–38" above stair nosings; accessible WC centerline is 16"–18" from the side wall (and 17"–19" seat height AFF); and a 60" turning circle is required. C is false (maximum accessible ramp slope is 1:12 or 8.33%, with max 30" rise per run); E is false (bottom handrail extension is one tread depth sloping plus 12" horizontal in ADA 2010, or one tread depth in IBC); F is false (commercial guards must be at least 42" high).
questions.reference: NCARB Handbook p. 124 (ADA Standards & IBC)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 6 (Question 511, p. 6-2)
questions.stem: Which of the following field tests is used on a construction site to determine the workability and consistency of fresh concrete before placement?

options.text: Steiner tunnel test (ASTM E84)
28-day concrete cylinder compression test (ASTM C39)
Electrical impedance moisture test
Kelly ball test (or Slump Cone test ASTM C143)

questions.explanation: Both the standard Slump Cone test (ASTM C143) and the Kelly Ball penetration test (ASTM C360) measure the consistency and workability of freshly mixed concrete in the field. The cylinder test measures compressive strength of cured concrete, and the Steiner tunnel test (ASTM E84) measures flame-spread and smoke-developed indices of interior finishes.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 6.pdf (Question 511, p. 6-2)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 6 (Question 512, p. 6-2)
questions.stem: During which period in the curing process does normal Portland cement concrete gain the most rapid rate of compressive strength (typically reaching ~65–70% of its 28-day design strength by the end of the first week)?

options.text: 0–7 days (specifically highest daily rate in the first 3–7 days)
14–21 days
21–28 days
28–56 days

questions.explanation: Concrete hydration is exothermic and fastest immediately after mixing: normal concrete reaches roughly 40–50% of its design strength in 0–3 days and 65–70% by 7 days, tapering off logarithmically toward 100% of design f'c at 28 days.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 6.pdf (Question 512, p. 6-2)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 6 (Question 514, p. 6-2)
questions.stem: Which device is mounted in an exterior doorway to depressurize (or pressurize) a building enclosure to 50 Pascals and measure whole-building air infiltration/leakage during commissioning?

options.text: Incline manometer only
Blower door assembly
Balometer flow hood
Duct blaster tester

questions.explanation: A Blower Door assembly mounts a calibrated variable-speed fan and pressure gauges in an exterior door frame to pressurize or depressurize the building envelope (typically to 50 Pa) to quantify air leakage (ACH50) and locate envelope leaks with infrared thermography or smoke pencils.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 6.pdf (Question 514, p. 6-2)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 6 (Question 516, p. 6-2)
questions.stem: During a Post-Occupancy Evaluation (POE) of a newly occupied office building, several employees report headaches and eye irritation that disappear shortly after they leave the building each evening. Which THREE statements are correct regarding Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) and Building-Related Illness (BRI)?

options.text: Off-gassing of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from new adhesives, carpets, and furniture is a primary contributor to Sick Building Syndrome.
Insufficient outdoor air ventilation in areas with high concentrations of odors or chemicals can cause nausea, dizziness, and headaches.
Radon and friable asbestos cause acute Sick Building Syndrome symptoms that resolve immediately upon leaving the building.
Sick Building Syndrome causes permanent symptoms that continue indefinitely after occupants leave the building.
Legionnaires' disease (from contaminated cooling tower/HVAC water) is classified as a Building-Related Illness (BRI), not Sick Building Syndrome.
Sick Building Syndrome can always be traced to a single clinically diagnosable pathogen.

questions.explanation: Sick Building Syndrome (SBS) describes acute discomfort (headaches, eye/throat irritation, fatigue) linked to time spent in a building—often caused by VOC off-gassing (A) and inadequate outdoor air ventilation (B)—where symptoms typically subside after leaving the building. By contrast, Building-Related Illness (BRI), such as Legionnaires' disease (E), has a specific, clinically diagnosable cause and symptoms that persist after leaving the building.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 6.pdf (Question 516, p. 6-2)

questions.source: Case Study CS-CE-1 (AIA G702 Payment Application #4)
questions.stem: Refer to AIA Document G702 Payment Application #4 in Case Study CS-CE-1. The Contract Sum to Date is $6,000,000. Total Work Completed and Stored to Date is $2,800,000, subject to a 10% retainage across both completed work and stored materials. Given that Previous Certificates for Payment (Apps #1–#3) totaled $1,920,000, what is the exact Current Payment Due (Line 8) that the Architect should certify?
questions.explanation: Per AIA G702: Total Completed & Stored to Date (Line 4) = $2,800,000. Less 10% Retainage (Line 5 = $280,000) gives Total Earned Less Retainage (Line 6) = $2,520,000. Subtracting Less Previous Certificates for Payment (Line 7 = $1,920,000) yields Current Payment Due (Line 8) = $600,000.
questions.reference: Case Study CS-CE-1 & PCM Study Guide_RMS.pdf (How contractor gets paid)

questions.source: Case Study CS-CE-1 & AIA A201-2017 Article 7
questions.stem: Match each AIA construction administration document to its purpose and required signatures under AIA A201-2017.
tokens: AIA G704 — Certificate of Substantial Completion

targets.label: Modifies Contract Sum/Time by mutual agreement; signed by Owner, Architect, AND Contractor
Directs immediate change in Work when price is not yet agreed; signed by Owner & Architect
Orders minor change in Work with NO change to Contract Sum or Time; signed by Architect ONLY
Establishes date when Owner can occupy space for intended use & starts warranty period
targets.correctToken: AIA G704 — Certificate of Substantial Completion

questions.explanation: Mastering the 4 G-series forms is essential for CE and PjM: G701 (Change Order: 3 signatures), G714 (CCD: Owner + Architect signatures when price is disputed), G710 (ASI: Architect signature only, zero cost/time impact), and G704 (Substantial Completion: prepared by Architect after inspection, triggers warranties and transfers utilities/insurance to Owner).

questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 6 (Question 1 & 2, p. 1-1)
questions.stem: Two days before sealed bids are due on a municipal public library project, a prospective bidder submits a question identifying a discrepancy between the door hardware schedule and the life-safety egress plan. How should the Architect communicate the binding clarification to all prospective bidders prior to the bid opening?

options.text: Issue an Architect's Supplemental Instruction (AIA G710) to the bidder who asked the question
Issue a written Addendum to all registered bidding document holders prior to receipt of bids
Execute Change Order #1 (AIA G701) immediately
Reply verbally by phone to the bidder to keep the bid schedule on track

questions.explanation: Prior to the opening of bids and execution of the construction contract, any modification, clarification, or correction to the Bidding Documents must be issued as a written Addendum sent to all prospective bidders who have received Bidding Documents (AIA A701). ASIs and Change Orders are only used AFTER the construction contract is executed.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 6.pdf & PPI Review Manual_Division 6.pdf

questions.source: AIA A201-2017 Section 3.12 & 4.2.7 (Submittals)
questions.stem: A structural steel subcontractor sends structural connection shop drawings directly to the Architect for review to save time. Upon opening the transmittal, the Architect notices the General Contractor has not reviewed or stamped the shop drawings. Under AIA Document A201-2017 Section 3.12, what action should the Architect take?

options.text: Review and approve the shop drawings immediately to prevent delaying the Critical Path.
Forward the shop drawings directly to the structural engineer for stamping and return them to the subcontractor.
Return the shop drawings to the General Contractor without action, because the Contractor must first review and approve all submittals for field dimensions and coordination.
Issue a Stop Work Order on the structural steel fabrication plant.

questions.explanation: Under AIA A201-2017 Section 3.12.5 and 4.2.7, the Contractor must review and approve all Submittals for compliance with the Contract Documents before submitting them to the Architect. Submittals that are not marked as reviewed and approved by the General Contractor may be returned by the Architect without action.
questions.reference: PPI Review Manual_Division 6.pdf (Submittals & Shop Drawings)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 5)
questions.stem: An architect is calculating the net floor area for an office complex with a client. The building houses 11 water closets scattered throughout the 75,680 gross-square-foot, single-story building. Using a standard commercial office net-to-gross efficiency factor of 80% and subtracting the 11 non-assignable water closets (at 50 SF each = 550 SF), what is the resulting net programmable square footage of the building?
questions.explanation: From Walking the ARE 2.1 (Q5): Taking the 75,680 GSF less the 550 SF of water closets = 75,130 SF × 0.80 office efficiency factor = 60,104 NSF.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 5, p. 33 & p. 67)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 6)
questions.stem: A new-build senior living recreational center is in the early programming/planning stages, and the architect is working with the structural engineer to determine which structural roof/floor framing systems are suited to span a 40-foot open space in a Type IIB (noncombustible unprotected) building. Which THREE systems are feasible for a 40-ft span and Type IIB construction?

options.text: Dimension lumber wood joists
Glued-laminated timber beams
Open-web steel joists (OWSJ)
One-way flat reinforced concrete slab
Precast hollow-core concrete planks
Two-way concrete waffle slab

questions.explanation: Type IIB construction requires noncombustible structural elements (ruling out dimension wood joists A and glulam timber B for primary framing unless heavy timber exceptions apply, and dimension wood joists cannot span 40 ft). For a 40-foot clear span, Open-Web Steel Joists (C), Precast Hollow-Core Concrete Planks (E), and Two-Way Concrete Waffle Slabs (F) are all noncombustible systems capable of spanning 40 feet efficiently.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 6, p. 33)

questions.source: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 Practice Exam (Question 12)
questions.stem: An architect has been called to find a passive landscape/envelope solution to help keep summer air-conditioning utility costs down for an existing home located in Minneapolis, Minnesota, particularly during hot late-afternoon hours. Which strategy should the architect propose?

options.text: Plant dense coniferous evergreen trees directly in front of the south-facing windows
Install vertical shading fins (or plant deciduous shade trees) on the west-facing windows
Remove all north-facing windows
Replace interior hardwood floors with thick carpet over the concrete slab

questions.explanation: Low-angle late-afternoon summer sun comes from the WEST (and east in the morning), where horizontal overhangs are ineffective. Installing vertical shading fins on west-facing windows blocks low-angle western summer solar heat gain while preserving views. Planting evergreen trees on the south (A) would block desirable winter passive solar heating in Minneapolis.
questions.reference: PA Walking the ARE 2.1 practice exam.pdf (Question 12, p. 34)

questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 5/4 (Stormwater & Site Design)
questions.stem: An architect is designing a suburban corporate campus on a previously undeveloped site and wants to minimize post-development stormwater runoff volume and peak discharge rate while promoting groundwater recharge. Which combination of strategies is most effective?

options.text: Increase asphalt parking lot slope to 5% and discharge directly into municipal storm sewers
Minimize impervious building/paving footprint, use pervious paving in parking stalls, and integrate vegetated bioswales and retention basins
Specify a dark EPDM membrane roof with oversized PVC roof leaders
Grade the entire site uniformly at 0.25% slope without swales

questions.explanation: Reducing the Rational Method runoff coefficient (C) in Q = C·i·A requires minimizing impervious surfaces, utilizing pervious pavements, vegetated green roofs, and bioswales/bioretention cells that slow runoff velocity and promote on-site infiltration.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf (Problem 4, p. 3-1)

questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 5 (Problem 6 — Lighting)
questions.stem: An architect is selecting an interior architectural lighting system for a university computer drafting and visualization lab where eliminating veiled reflections and screen glare on vertical/angled monitors is the top priority. Which luminaire distribution type is most desirable?

options.text: Direct unshielded downlighting with specular parabolic louvers directly over desks
Indirect or direct-indirect pendant luminaires bouncing uniform illumination off a high-reflectance acoustic ceiling
High-bay metal halide point-source floodlights
Low-mounted wall sconces only

questions.explanation: Indirect (90–100% upward light) or semi-indirect pendant luminaires illuminate the ceiling plane uniformly, eliminating high-luminance point reflections (veiling reflections and glare) on computer screens.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf (Problem 6, p. 3-1)

questions.section: Section 1: Integration of Building Materials & Systems
questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 5 (Masonry Cleaning & Efflorescence)
questions.stem: Shortly after construction of a new clay brick veneer wall, white powdery crystalline deposits (efflorescence) appear on the face of the brick. Which initial cleaning procedure should the architect specify to remove the efflorescence without etching the brick or mortar joints?

options.text: High-pressure sandblasting at 3,000 psi
Dry stiff-bristle non-metallic brushing with clear water rinse (avoiding harsh muriatic acid solutions)
Pressure washing with a 25% unbuffered hydrochloric (muriatic) acid solution
Applying an impermeable silicone film coating over the wet brick

questions.explanation: Efflorescence consists of water-soluble salts brought to the surface as moisture evaporates. It should be removed with a dry stiff-bristle brush and low-pressure water wash. Acid washing (muriatic acid) or high-pressure sandblasting damages the protective fired skin of the brick and dissolves mortar joints.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 5.pdf (p. 500 / 669 Solutions)

questions.source: PPI Practice Exam Division 6 (Question 513, p. 6-2)
questions.stem: Before excavation begins, the building footprint and foundation wall offset lines are laid out by a surveyor and preserved outside the limits of excavation using wooden frameworks that hold taut string lines at a constant elevation. What are these offset wooden frameworks called?

options.text: Grade stakes
Batter boards
Property corner pins
Benchmark monuments

questions.explanation: Corner stakes placed at the exact building corners would be destroyed as soon as excavation starts. Therefore, wooden 'batter boards' are erected 4 to 6 feet outside the excavation limits so string lines can be stretched between them to re-establish exact foundation corners and elevations during excavation and footing layout.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Exam_Division 6.pdf (Question 513, p. 6-2)

questions.source: PPI Practice Problems Division 6 (Problem 3, p. 1-1)
questions.stem: An architect has been hired as a consultant to a Design-Build entity under AIA Document B143. During construction of the foundation, the Owner visits the site and verbally instructs the Architect to relocate a loading dock door by 12 feet. How should the Architect respond?

options.text: Issue an ASI (G710) directly to the concrete trade contractor immediately.
Inform the Owner that in a Design-Build delivery method, all Owner directives and scope changes must flow through the Design-Builder, with whom both the Owner and Architect hold their contracts.
Execute a Change Order with the subcontractor on the spot.
Instruct the structural engineer to redesign the foundation wall at the Architect's expense.

questions.explanation: In a Design-Build delivery method where the Architect is contracted to the Design-Builder (AIA B143), the Architect has no direct contractual relationship with the Owner. All communication, change requests, and authorizations from the Owner must be directed through the Design-Builder.
questions.reference: PPI Practice Problems_Division 6.pdf (Problem 3, p. 1-1)
